John Preston Griffith, of Smith & Griffith, LLP, of
Anderson; Christopher James Moore, of Richardson
Thomas, LLC, of Florence; and Grace Madeline

C. Mitchell Brown, Rachel Atkin Hedley, and Allen
Mattison Bogan, all of Nelson Mullins Riley &
Scarborough, LLP, of Columbia, for Respondent.
JUSTICE HILL: Anderson resident Reid Fleming alleges he was burned when the
model 18650 lithium-ion battery in his vape pen exploded. His injury occurred in
Charleston. Fleming claims LG Chem, Ltd. (LG) manufactured the battery, which
he bought in Charleston from The Planet Vape, LLC. Fleming sued LG, Planet
Vape, and others in South Carolina circuit court for his injuries. LG moved to
dismiss Fleming's claim against it, contending South Carolina lacked personal
jurisdiction. The trial court granted LG's motion, and the court of appeals affirmed,
with Judge Hewitt dissenting. Fleming v. Planet Vape, LLC, Op. No. 2025-UP-295
(S.C. Ct. App. filed August 13, 2025).
We granted Fleming's petition for writ of certiorari to consider whether due process
permits LG to be subject to personal jurisdiction in South Carolina under the
circumstances here. We hold it does.
I. Fleming's Complaint
LG is a South Korean corporation with its principal offices located in Seoul. Its
consumer electronics business spans the globe. In his complaint, Fleming alleges
LG has numerous contacts with South Carolina. According to Fleming, these
contacts relate to his claims because LG manufactures lithium-ion batteries knowing
they will be distributed and sold in South Carolina to individuals who will use them
to power vape pens. Despite this knowledge, LG has done "virtually nothing to
prevent its lithium-ion battery products from being sold individually throughout the
United States and, specifically, in South Carolina." Fleming claims LG continued
this distribution scheme knowing vaping devices in which its lithium-ion batteries
were being used lack adequate circuitry and other safety protections. He further
alleges LG knows its lithium-ion batteries are being rewrapped by its commercial
customers and being sold throughout the United States and online for individual use.
Fleming's complaint listed five cases pending in South Carolina where the circuit
court has exercised personal jurisdiction over LG in similar lawsuits involving
individuals injured by LG lithium-ion batteries used to power vape pens. He also
contends LG has consented to personal jurisdiction in a federal court action in South
Carolina involving an exploding lithium-ion battery.
II. Personal Jurisdiction: The Long Arm Statute and Due Process
A court may only exert its jurisdictional power when that power has been
legislatively granted and does not exceed constitutional limits. Accordingly,
determining whether a South Carolina court has personal jurisdiction over a non-
resident defendant involves two inquiries. S. Plastics Co. v. S. Com. Bank, 310 S.C.
256, 259, 423 S.E.2d 128, 130 (1992). The first inquiry—which asks whether the
jurisdictional reach of our long-arm statute extends to the defendant's conduct—is
not at issue here. The second inquiry asks if exercising personal jurisdiction over
the defendant comports with the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.
See U.S. Const. amend. XIV. This is the familiar world still governed by the
landmark decision in International Shoe, which held that due process allows a court
to exercise personal jurisdiction over a non-resident defendant when the defendant
has enough "minimum contacts" with the forum state to make the state's jurisdiction
reasonable in the sense that it "does not offend 'traditional notions of fair play and
substantial justice.'" Int'l Shoe Co. v. Washington, 326 U.S. 310, 316–17 (1945)
(quoting Milliken v. Meyer, 311 U.S. 457, 463 (1941)).
III. Standard of Review
To survive a motion to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction, a plaintiff bears "the
burden of proving personal jurisdiction over a nonresident" by making "a prima facie
showing of jurisdiction either in the complaint or in affidavits." Cockrell v. Hillerich
& Bradsby Co., 363 S.C. 485, 491, 611 S.E.2d 505, 508 (2005). We must affirm a
trial court's personal jurisdiction ruling unless it has no factual support or was the
result of an error of law. See Atl. Soft Drink Co. of Columbia v. S.C. Nat'l Bank, 287
S.C. 228, 233, 336 S.E.2d 876, 879 (1985).
IV. General and Specific Personal Jurisdiction: The Framework
There are two types of personal jurisdiction: general and specific. A court has
general (or "all purpose") jurisdiction over an individual in the state of his domicile
and over a corporation in its state of incorporation and the state where it has its
principal place of business. Daimler AG v. Bauman, 571 U.S. 117, 137 (2014). As
its name implies, general jurisdiction is broad—in most instances, a court that has
general jurisdiction over a defendant may hear cases of any type against that
defendant, regardless of where the conduct occurred or the claim arose.
This case turns on specific jurisdiction. A court has specific (or "case-linked")
jurisdiction over a non-resident defendant when the claim has a sufficient connection
to the forum state. The sufficiency of the connection depends upon the relationship
between the defendant, the forum, and the claim. For specific jurisdiction to attach,
three conditions must be met. Burger King Corp. v. Rudzewicz, 471 U.S. 462, 472–
78 (1985). First, the defendant must have "purposefully avail[ed] itself of the
privilege of conducting activities within the forum state, thus invoking the benefits
and protections of its laws." Hanson v. Denckla, 357 U.S. 235, 253 (1958). The
requisite contacts cannot be random, nor can they be generated by the unilateral
actions of a third party.
Second, the claim must "arise out of or relate to" the defendant's contacts with the
forum state. Ford Motor Co. v. Montana Eighth Jud. Dist. Ct., 592 U.S. 351, 359
(2021) (quoting Bristol-Myers Squibb Co. v. Superior Ct. of California, San
Francisco Cnty., 582 U.S. 255, 262 (2017)). That is, there must be a link between
the forum and the claims, typically an activity or occurrence that took place in the
forum state. Id. at 359–60.
Third, the exercise of personal jurisdiction over the defendant must comply with the
fundamental fairness that due process guarantees, which International Shoe
expressed as "the traditional notions of fair play and substantial justice."
V. LG's Arguments Against Specific Personal Jurisdiction
LG does not dispute that, by its commercial presence here, it has purposefully
availed itself of doing business in South Carolina markets. It stridently disputes,
however, the second specific jurisdiction requirement: that Fleming's claims arise
out of or relate to LG's South Carolina contacts. LG presses two main arguments.
The first attacks the allegations of Fleming's complaint that LG has distributed or
sold 18650 lithium-ion batteries in South Carolina. The second maintains that
because LG only designs, markets, and sells 18650 batteries in multi-packs to
commercial customers for use as component parts and does not distribute or sell
individual batteries directly to consumers for personal use, Fleming's injury cannot
arise out of or relate to LG's South Carolina contacts.
A. Fleming's Complaint and LG's Distribution of 18650 Batteries in South
Carolina
Fleming's complaint states he was injured by an LG lithium-ion battery and LG has
systematically and continuously sold lithium-ion batteries in South Carolina. LG
counters that Fleming has not shown LG's contacts include distribution or sale of the
18650 lithium-ion battery. According to LG, this absence of evidence is evidence
of the absence of the minimum contacts needed to justify jurisdiction. This argument
suffers from the fatal logical fallacy known as an appeal to ignorance. Easily
identified in the wild by its missing logical step, the fallacy is to assume something
is false because it has not been proven true, and vice versa. Mercifully, its lifespan
is brief in most legal contexts because, as here, it conflicts with the applicable burden
of proof.
The hole in LG's logic is its assumption, without proof, that Fleming's description of
LG's lithium-ion battery activity does not encompass 18650 lithium-ion batteries.
Although it attacks Fleming's jurisdictional allegations as overbroad, it does not
deny them. Nowhere does LG deny that it serves the South Carolina market with
lithium-ion batteries, and nowhere does it deny that this includes the 18650 type.
This non-denial did not flip the burden back to Fleming and require him to prove
that which was never denied. Even if Fleming's general grouping of all lithium-ion
batteries left room for some factual dispute about its scope, at the pleading stage we
are obligated to resolve that dispute in favor of Fleming, not LG. See Brown v. Inv.
Mgmt. & Rsch., Inc., 323 S.C. 395, 399, 475 S.E.2d 754, 756 (1996) ("Courts will
take as true the allegations of the nonmoving party and resolve all factual disputes
in its favor." (quoting 5A Charles A. Wright & Arthur R. Miller, Federal Practice
and Procedure § 1351 (Supp. 1995))).
B. LG and Individual Consumer Use of LG 18650 Batteries
In its second argument attacking relatedness, LG contends it has never designed,
marketed, distributed, or sold lithium-ion 18650 batteries for personal consumer use
anywhere, much less in South Carolina. It filed an affidavit stating it sells them only
to commercial customers in packs for use as component parts and never to individual
consumers for personal use. Therefore, so LG's theory goes, Fleming's injury was
not caused by LG's conduct but by the unilateral actions of rogue sellers who
somehow obtained the packs, broke them open, and sold single batteries to
consumers. Therefore, according to LG, Fleming's claims cannot "arise out of or
relate to" its contacts or activity within South Carolina.
LG's argument rests on a causation theory the United States Supreme Court rejected
in Ford. In that case, Ford Motor Company insisted it could not be subject to
personal jurisdiction in a state just because its vehicles caused an injury in that state.
Instead, specific jurisdiction would be proper only in a forum where Ford's conduct
giving rise to the plaintiff's claim occurred, either where the car was sold or where
it was designed and manufactured. Ford urged that the location of the injury
occurred was irrelevant for personal jurisdiction purposes when Ford's conduct that
caused the injury occurred outside of that state.
Rejecting Ford's arguments, the Court emphasized that "[n]one of our precedents has
suggested that only a strict causal relationship between the defendant's in-state
activity and the litigation will do." Ford, 592 U.S. at 362. The court explained that
a defendant's relationship with a forum state may be enough to support specific
jurisdiction even when there is no proof the plaintiff's claim was caused by the
defendant's in-state conduct. Id. Put another way, an injury may arise out of or be
related to a defendant's contacts even though those contacts did not cause the injury.
The distinction the Ford Court draws between causation and relatedness is sublime,
to say the least. It can perhaps be better understood by remembering that the
touchstone of due process in personal jurisdiction is that an out of state defendant
must have "fair warning" that its activity affecting the forum state may subject it to
being held accountable in that state for related conduct. Burger King Corp., 471
U.S. at 471–72. Fair warning may exist even though the occurrence or activity is
not caused by—but nevertheless arises out of or is related to—the defendant's forum
state contacts.
Although the second or relatedness prong of specific jurisdiction does not demand
that the injury would not have happened but for the defendant's in-state conduct, we
must still examine what the level of relatedness must be. It has long been the law
that specific jurisdiction does not lie over a corporation that, although it may have
systematically and continuously conducted activities in the forum state, did nothing
in that state that relates to the plaintiff's claims. Rather, for specific jurisdiction to
attach, there must be some affiliation between the forum and the litigation,
"principally, activity or an occurrence that takes place in the forum state and is
therefore subject to the State's regulation." Goodyear Dunlop Tires Operations, S.A.
v. Brown, 564 U.S. 915, 919 (2011). This is consistent with the observation in
International Shoe that even single or occasional acts of a corporation in a state
"because of their nature and quality and the circumstances of their commission, may
be deemed sufficient to render the corporation liable to suit." 326 U.S. at 318.
We need not dwell on the far end of the relatedness continuum, for the complaint
demonstrates that LG's activity would meet even a strict causation standard. Ford
reaffirmed the principle that specific jurisdiction may be found when a company
"serves a market for a product in the forum state and the product malfunctions there."
Ford, 592 U.S. at 363. The Court did not hedge on this vital point. Its statement
was not limited to or conditioned upon whether the injury was caused by the intended
use of the product.
Applying this principle is enough for us to decide that LG is subject to specific
personal jurisdiction here. Taking, as we must, Fleming's allegations as true that LG
has systematically and continuously served the lithium-ion battery market in South
Carolina (including the 18650 market), there is little doubt that the occurrence—
Fleming's injury—arises out of and is related to LG's activity here. After all, a
corporation's minimum contacts in a forum state "has never been doubted when the
activities of the corporation there have not only been continuous and systematic, but
also give rise to the liabilities sued on." Int'l Shoe, 326 U.S. at 317.
Also, for purposes of due process, where the injury occurred or who was injured is
relevant. The forum state's interest in exercising jurisdiction intensifies if the injury
occurred in that state and the injury is to one of its citizens. This location connection
goes to the due process concern that the state's jurisdiction be reasonable, which
acknowledges that states have a profound interest in the orderly administration of
their laws. These interests do not wane when the injury occurred by an unintended
use of an out of state company's product to a person outside the company's intended
market. For example, if a battery pack had exploded in South Carolina while in the
back of a truck delivering a shipment of batteries to a South Carolina business and
injuring the truck driver and bystanders, LG could hardly argue that the injuries did
not arise out of or relate to its activity in South Carolina because the truck driver and
the bystanders were not intended users of the product. A non-resident defendant
who has raked in profits by exploiting a state's business market with a product may
not escape jurisdiction by claiming the injury arose out of the unintended use of the
product or caused damage to someone other than an intended user. Such a
jurisdictional rule would be as artificial as it is unprecedented and unfair.
At any rate, the complaint alleges LG not only knew about the widespread use of its
individual lithium-ion batteries by consumers in vaping pens, but it also did little to
deter such use, even after it knew these uses were resulting in malfunctions causing
grave injury in this state.
Although, without more, "the place of a plaintiff's injury and residence cannot create
a defendant's contact with the forum state," those places "may be relevant in
assessing the link between the defendant's forum contacts and the plaintiff's suit—
including its assertions of who was injured where." Ford, 592 U.S. at 371. Like the
plaintiffs in Ford, here, Fleming "brought suit in the most natural State—based on
an 'affiliation between the forum and the underlying controversy, principally [an]
activity or an occurrence that t[ook] place' there." Id. at 370 (quoting Bristol-Myers
Squibb Co., 582 U.S. at 262).
We are aware that other courts have confronted similar jurisdictional arguments by
LG and other battery manufacturers. Some have found personal jurisdiction exists,
others have not. Compare L.G. Chem America, Inc. v. Morgan, 670 S.W.3d 341,
351 (Tex. 2023) (holding LG's contacts with Texas were enough to satisfy due
process for personal jurisdiction purposes), and Sullivan v. LG Chem, LTD., 79 F.4th
651, 674 (6th Cir. 2023) (holding a Michigan federal district court had personal
jurisdiction over LG), with Yamashita v. LG Chem, Ltd., 62 F.4th 496, 507–09 (9th
Cir. 2023) (finding the plaintiff did not satisfy his burden of proof for personal
jurisdiction and noting LG's contacts with Hawaii were sales of 18650 batteries to
manufacturers, not stand-alone battery sales to individual consumers).
One of the most recent and prominent is B.D. ex rel. Myers v. Samsung Sdi Co., 143
F.4th 757 (7th Cir. 2025). There, the Seventh Circuit held that Indiana could not
exercise specific jurisdiction over Samsung in a case involving an 18650 lithium-ion
battery that exploded in an Indiana resident's pocket and injured him in Indiana. The
Seventh Circuit fashioned a specific jurisdiction test focusing on whether the non-
resident defendant had availed itself of Indiana's forum by delivering its products
into the stream of commerce expecting Indiana consumers would purchase them. At
this level of generality, the test follows World-Wide Volkswagen Corp. v, Woodson,
444 U.S. 286 (1980), scrupulously. The Seventh Circuit went on, though, to refine
the test by separating the stream of commerce into two currents, or what it called the
"end-product" stream and the "derivative-product" stream. B.D., 143 F.4th at 767.
The "end-product" stream denoted 18650 battery packs Samsung marketed and sold
as component parts to commercial customers, while the "derivative product" stream
was consisted of individual 18650 batteries third parties had broken off from the
packs and resold to individuals outside of Samsung's intended distribution chain. Id.
at 767–69. The Seventh Circuit held that because the plaintiff was injured by the
derivative product, his claim did not arise out of and was not related to Samsung's
Indiana contacts. Id. at 772–73. Therefore, specific jurisdiction over Samsung was
lacking. Id. at 775; see also Ethridge v. Samsung SDI Co., Ltd., 163 F.4th 136, 139
(5th Cir. 2025) (following the Seventh Circuit's approach in Myers); Franceschi v.
LG Chem, Ltd., 580 P.3d 1279, 1284–86 (Nev. 2025) (same).
With much respect, we find this separatist approach—or intended market
approach—too formalistic. International Shoe warned of the folly of focusing on
mechanical or quantitative approaches to personal jurisdiction. 326 U.S. at 319; see
also Burger King Corp., 471 U.S. at 478 ("The Court long ago rejected the notion
that personal jurisdiction might turn on 'mechanical' tests, or on 'conceptualistic . . .
theories of the place of contracting or of performance.'") (citations omitted) (quoting
Int'l Shoe, 326 U.S. at 319; Hoopeston Canning Co. v. Cullen, 318 U.S. 313, 316
(1943)). Perhaps courts could, with their visible pens, sort what the invisible hand
has unsorted in the marketplace. But such an effort would remove adjudication from
the reality of economic markets. Products have ways of finding markets far afield
of those their creators envisioned. When a company learns of such secondary
markets and continues to indirectly supply them, such activity also supplies the
contacts necessary to support personal jurisdiction over the company in lawsuits that
arise out of or are related to that activity.
The intended market approach is just another way to impose a strict causation
requirement on the specific jurisdiction test. This approach in essence says that an
occurrence that takes place in the forum state does not count as a contact by the non-
resident defendant for jurisdictional purposes unless the occurrence was caused by
the intended scope of the non-resident's activity.
In any event, the intended market approach would not help LG here. Fleming has
made a prima facie showing that LG's conduct demonstrates an intent to serve the
South Carolina market for individual 18650 batteries used in vaping devices. LG is
correct that the mere foreseeability that its product may end up in South Carolina is
not enough to justify jurisdiction. Yet, foreseeability can still be relevant, for "the
foreseeability that is critical to due process is not the mere likelihood that a product
will find its way into the forum State. Rather it is that the defendant's conduct and
connection with the forum state are such that he should reasonably anticipate being
haled into court there." World-Wide Volkswagen, 444 U.S. at 287. The Court in
World-Wide Volkswagen further explained:
Hence if the sale of a product of a manufacturer or distributor . . . is not
simply an isolated occurrence, but arises from the efforts of the
manufacturer or distributor to serve directly or indirectly, the market
for its product in other States, it is not unreasonable to subject it to suit
in one of those States if its allegedly defective merchandise has there
been the source of injury to its owner or to others. The forum State does
not exceed its powers under the Due Process Clause if it asserts
personal jurisdiction over a corporation that delivers its products into
the stream of commerce with the expectation that they will be
purchased by consumers in the forum State.
Id. at 297–98. We have followed this expression of the stream of commerce theory.
State v. NV Sumatra Tobacco Trading, Co., 379 S.C. 81, 89–91, 666 S.E.2d 218,
222 (2008).
Fleming has made a prima facie showing that LG has placed lithium-ion batteries in
the stream of commerce knowing they will reach South Carolina and be sold
individually to consumers here. He has further shown that LG knows these sales
have caused injury to individual consumers and knows it has been repeatedly sued
in the courts of this state for injuries arising out of such individual use. These
showings suggest LG's intended market in fact includes individuals seeking to buy
lithium-ion batteries for use in vaping devices. They also fortify our conclusion that
LG received ample "fair warning" that it may have to defend itself in South Carolina
courts for its related conduct here.
We are far removed from the situation where the stream of commerce, aided by the
efforts of third parties, has swept the non-resident defendant's product into a forum
without the defendant's knowledge or design. Fleming's allegations demonstrate that
LG has continued to profit from distributing its products while knowing its
distribution stream has been compromised.
In sum, LG's contacts with South Carolina that relate to Fleming's injury are not
random or fortuitous. It does not offend due process to require LG to defend itself
in a forum where it has known its products have been sold and wreaked injury.
c. Fair Play and Substantial Justice
The third and last aspect of specific jurisdiction we must resolve brings us back to
the overarching directive that the non-resident's contacts with the forum state must
be extensive enough so that the exercise of jurisdiction is fundamentally fair to LG,
meaning it is consistent with traditional due process notions of fair play and
substantial justice. Chase Secs. Corp. v. Donaldson, 325 U.S. 304, 316–17 (1945).
By its wide operation in the South Carolina lithium-ion battery market, LG benefits
from the protection of our laws that empower LG to defend its property rights,
enforce its contracts, and create the hospitable market in which it has chosen to sell
its lithium-ion batteries. This places a reciprocal obligation on LG to comply with
the laws of that state that regulate its conduct and protect the safety of the state's
citizens. Under such circumstances, it can be neither unfair, unjust, nor surprising
to LG to be subject to suit here to enforce these obligations. And principles of
interstate federalism support allowing jurisdiction here to advance South Carolina's
legitimate interests in enforcing our own laws and providing our resident citizens
with a convenient forum to seek compensation for injuries inflicted on our resident
citizens by non-residents who have conducted significant activity here related to
those injuries.
Finally, allowing LG to evade jurisdiction here would allow it to distribute and sell
goods in the South Carolina market without complying with the same safety laws
and regulations that other companies doing business here must honor.
VI. Conclusion
Because we conclude South Carolina may exert specific personal jurisdiction over
LG in this case, the rulings of the trial court and the court of appeals are
REVERSED.
KITTREDGE, C.J., JAMES, VERDIN, JJ., and Acting Justice Daniel Dewitt
Hall, concur.
